(p-5) **Surah al-Ma'idah**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fulfil the contracts﴾. On this there are five opinions:

The first: they are the covenants of Allah, which faith binds upon His servants concerning what He has made lawful for them and what He has made unlawful for them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the covenants that Allah, Exalted is He, took from the People of the Book, that they would act upon what is in the Torah and the Gospel, including affirming Muhammad ﷺ. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The third: they are the covenants of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance), namely the alliance that existed among them. This is the view of Qatadah.

(p-6) The fourth: they are all the covenants of the religion. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The fifth: they are the contracts that people conclude among themselves, such as sale or marriage, or what a person binds upon himself, such as a vow or an oath. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

﴿Lawful for you is the beast of cattle﴾. On this there are three opinions:

The first: it refers to all livestock, namely camels, cattle and sheep. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: it refers to the unborn young of livestock that are found dead in the wombs of their mothers when the mothers are slaughtered or sacrificed. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar.

The third: the "beast of cattle" refers to the wild ones among them, such as gazelles and wild oxen, and it does not include the solid-hoofed animals, because the word is derived from *ni'mat al-wat'* (the blessing of copulation, i.e., the animal's capacity for breeding).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the sacred symbols of Allah﴾. That is, the markers of Allah. It is derived from *al-ish'ar*, which means informing or making known.

Concerning "the sacred symbols of Allah" there are five interpretations:

The first: they are the rites of the Hajj. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: they are what Allah has forbidden during the state of ihram (ritual consecration). This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are the sanctuary (haram) of Allah. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fourth: they are the limits of Allah concerning what He has made lawful and unlawful, permitted and prohibited. This is the view of 'Ata'.

The fifth: they are the entire religion of Allah. This is the view of al-Hasan, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is so; and whoever honours the sacred symbols of Allah, indeed it is from the piety of hearts﴾ [al-Hajj: 22], meaning the religion of Allah.

﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, that is, do not regard fighting in it as lawful. On this there are three opinions:

The first: it is Rajab of Mudar.

(p-7) The second: it is Dhu al-Qa'dah. This is the view of 'Ikrimah.

The third: it refers to the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum) in general. This is the view of Qatadah.

﴿Nor the sacrificial animals, nor the garlands﴾. As for the sacrificial animals (al-hady), there are two opinions:

One: it is whatever a person offers of anything to the House of Allah, Exalted is He.

The other: it is the livestock that has not been garlanded, when a person has vowed to offer it and garland it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

As for the garlands (al-qala'id), there are three opinions: They are the garlands of the sacrificial animals. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who held that when a person garlands his sacrificial animal he becomes a muhrim (one in the state of ihram).

The second: they are garlands made of tree bark, which the polytheists used to hang when they intended the Hajj, on their journey to Makkah and their return, so that they would be safe. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: the polytheists used to take tree bark from the sanctuary when they wished to leave it, and they would wear it as a garland so that they would be safe. They were forbidden to strip the trees of the sanctuary to wear them. This is the view of 'Ata'.

﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾. That is, do not treat as lawful those who are intending the Sacred House. It is said: *amamtu kadha* (I intended such-and-such) when one sets out for it. Some say *yammamtu* (I turned toward it), as in the words of the poet:

*Indeed, when a land displeases me, I turn the chest of my camel toward another land.*

﴿Seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure﴾. On this there are two opinions: One: it is profit in trade. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar.

The other: it is reward. This is the view of Mujahid. ﴿And good pleasure﴾ means that Allah, may He be pleased with them, is pleased with their acts of worship (nusuk).

﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾. Although this is in the form of a command, it comes after a prohibition (p-8), and so it indicates the permissibility of hunting after leaving ihram, not obligation.

﴿And do not let the enmity of a people lead you﴾. On *yajrimannakum* there are two interpretations:

One: it means "do not lead you" or "do not move you". This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kisa'i, and Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad. It is said *jaramani fulan 'ala bughdika* (so-and-so moved me to hate you), meaning he drove me to it. The poet said:

*I struck Abu 'Uyaynah with a blow that drove the clan of Fazarah to be angry after it.*

The other: its meaning is "do not earn for you", as in *jaramtu 'ala ahli* (I earned for my family). This is the view of al-Farra'.

Concerning ﴿enmity of a people﴾ there are two interpretations: One: its meaning is the hatred of a people. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The other: the hostility of a people. This is the view of Qatadah.

Al-Suddi said: "This verse was revealed concerning al-Hutam ibn Hind al-Bakri, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked, 'To what do you call?' He informed him. The Prophet ﷺ had said to his companions, 'A man from Rabi'ah will enter upon you today, speaking with the tongue of a devil.' When the Prophet ﷺ informed him, he said, 'Give me time until I consult.' He left from his presence, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'He entered with the face of a disbeliever and left with the back of a treacherous one.' He passed by a herd of camels from the herds of Madinah, seized them, and drove off, chanting verses:

(p-9) *The night has wrapped it with the driver Hutam; he is not a shepherd of camels nor of sheep, nor a butcher upon a back and a saddle. They slept while the son of Hind did not sleep. He kept at them like a boy like a rod, thick of calves, smooth of foot.*

Then in the following year he came as a pilgrim, garlanding his sacrificial animal. The companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked permission to kill him, and this verse was revealed up to His saying ﴿coming to the Sacred House﴾. Some of his companions said to him, 'O Messenger of Allah, leave between us and him, for he is our companion.' He said, 'He has garlanded (his animal).'"

Then they differed concerning what was abrogated (naskh) from this verse, after their consensus (ijma') that some of it was abrogated, on three opinions:

The first: all of it is abrogated. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, who said: "Nothing from al-Ma'idah was abrogated except this verse."

The second: what was abrogated from it is ﴿nor the sacred month, nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: what was abrogated from it is what the Jahiliyyah used to wear as garlands of tree bark. This is the view of Mujahid.

When the Prophet ﷺ informed him, he said, 'Give me time until I consult.' He passed by a herd of camels from the herds of Madinah, seized them, and drove off, chanting verses:

(p-9) *The night has wrapped it with the driver Hutam; he is not a shepherd of camels nor of sheep, nor a butcher upon a back and a saddle. They slept while the son of Hind did not sleep. He kept at them like a boy like a rod, thick of calves, smooth of foot.*

The companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked permission to kill him, and this verse was revealed up to His saying ﴿coming to the Sacred House﴾. Some of his companions said to him, 'O Messenger of Allah, leave between us and him, for he is our companion.' He said, 'He has garlanded (his animal).'"

The first: all of it is abrogated. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, who said: "Nothing from al-Ma'idah was abrogated except this verse."

The second: what was abrogated from it is ﴿nor the sacred month, nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: what was abrogated from it is what the Jahiliyyah used to wear as garlands of tree bark. This is the view of Mujahid.

**The first opinion:** it refers to every creature that has a flowing soul (*nafs sa'ilah*) among the land animals and birds.

**The second opinion:** it refers to every land animal and bird that dies without being slaughtered (*dhakah*).

﴿And blood﴾: there are two opinions. The first is that what is forbidden of it is only that which is poured forth (*masfuh*), as in the words of God Most High: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾. The second is that all blood is forbidden, whether poured forth or not, except what the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) has specified as exempt, namely the liver and the spleen. According to the first opinion, fish is not forbidden; according to the second, it is forbidden.

﴿And the flesh of swine﴾: there are two opinions. The first is that the prohibition applies specifically to the flesh of swine and not to its fat. This is the opinion of Dawud (al-Zahiri). The second is that it covers the flesh and whatever fat or other matter is mixed with it. This is the opinion of the majority (al-Jumhur), and there is no difference between the domestic and the wild swine.

﴿And that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾: this means what is slaughtered for other than God, such as idols and images. Its root is from *istihlal al-sabi* (the crying out of a newborn when it is born from its mother's womb). From it also comes *ihlal al-muhrim* (the uttering of the call by the pilgrim in *hajj* and *'umrah*). Ibn Ahmar said:

*﻿Its riders call out at al-Farqad, as the pilgrim in ihram calls out (for 'umrah).*

﻿﴿And the strangled animal﴾: there are two opinions. The first is that it is one strangled by the hunter's cord or otherwise until it dies. This is the opinion of al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. The second is that it is the one that is bound, and then its strangler kills it.

﴿And the beaten animal﴾ is the one struck with a stick until it dies. It is said: "I struck it (*waqadtuha*), I strike it (*aqidhuha*) with a blow (*wqdan*), and I cause it to be beaten (*uqidhuha*) with a beating (*iqadhan*), when I beat it severely." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*A strong-kicking [she-camel] that strikes the young camel with her leg, a flinging one of the forelegs of the virgin [she-camels].*

﴿And the fallen animal﴾ is the one that falls from the top of a mountain or into a well until it dies.

﴿And the gored animal﴾ is the sheep that is gored by another until it dies.

﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered﴾: there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to the strangled animal and what follows it. This is the opinion of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Hasan, and the majority. The second is that it refers only to what the beast of prey has eaten. This is reported from the Zahiriyya.

Regarding the prey of a beast of prey that becomes lawful by slaughter (*dhakah*), there are two opinions. The first is that it must have an eye that blinks or a tail that moves. The second is that it must have a strong movement, not like the movement of one who is being slaughtered. This is the opinion of al-Shafi'i and Malik.

﴿And that you seek decision through the arrows﴾: its meaning is that you seek knowledge of what has been allotted or not allotted of provision or need by means of the arrows. These were three arrows (*qidah*), one of which had written on it: "My Lord has commanded me," another: "My Lord has forbidden me," and the third was blank with nothing written on it. When they wanted to travel or to go to war, they cast them and sought a decision. If the one with "My Lord has commanded me" came out, they did it; if the one with "My Lord has forbidden me" came out, they left it; and if the blank one came out, they repeated the drawing. God forbade this, and it was called *istiqsam* because they sought by it knowledge of what had been allotted to them.

Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad said: rather, it is derived from *qasam al-yamin* (the oath), because they bound themselves to what they bound themselves to by oath.

﴿That is a transgression﴾, that is, a departure from the command of God and His obedience, and doing what He had previously forbidden.

﴿This day those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾: there are two opinions. The first is that they despaired of your apostasy, that you would return to their religion. The second is that they despaired of being able to overturn it and to discredit its validity.

Mujahid said: this was on the day of 'Arafah, when the Prophet (ﷺ) performed the Farewell Pilgrimage (*hajjat al-wada'*), after the Arabs had entered Islam, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not see any polytheist.

﴿So do not fear them but fear Me﴾: that is, do not fear that they will prevail over you, and fear Me, lest you oppose My command.

﴿This day I have perfected for you your religion﴾: there are two opinions. The first is that it is the day of 'Arafah in the Farewell Pilgrimage, and the Messenger (ﷺ) did not live after that except eighty-one nights. This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second is that it refers to the whole time of the Prophet (ﷺ), until this was revealed to him on the day of 'Arafah. This is the opinion of al-Hasan.

Regarding the perfecting of the religion, there are two opinions. The first means: I have perfected My obligations, My limits, what is lawful and what is unlawful for you, and no obligation of permission or prohibition was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) after this. This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second means: this day I have perfected your pilgrimage for you, that you perform the Sacred House pilgrimage and no polytheist performs it with you. This is the opinion of Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾ by perfecting your religion.

﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾: that is, I have approved for you submission to My command as a religion, that is, obedience.

Qabisa reported that he said: "Ka'b said: If this verse had been revealed to any nation other than this Ummah, they would have magnified the day on which it was revealed to them and taken it as a festival in which they gather. Umar said: I know the day on which it was revealed and the place where it was revealed. It was revealed on the day of Friday and the day of 'Arafah, and both of them, praise be to God, are festivals for us."

﴿Then whoever is compelled﴾, that is, the harm of hunger has afflicted him.

﴿by severe hunger﴾, that is, in famine. It is a noun of place (*maf'alah*) like *majhalah*, *mabkhalah*, *majbanah*, and *makhzayah*, from *khamas al-batn* (the emptiness of the belly), which is his enduring hunger. Al-A'sha said:

*You spend the night in winter with your bellies full, while your neighbors, drowned [in sleep], spend the night with empty bellies.*

﴿without inclining toward sin﴾: there are two opinions. The first is without intentionally committing sin. This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid. The second is without leaning toward sin. Its root is from *janafa al-qawm* when they inclined. Every crooked thing among the Arabs is called *ajnaf*.

Al-Awza'i narrated from Hassan, from Atiyyah, from Abu Waqid al-Laythi, who said: "We said: O Messenger of God, we are in a land where we are afflicted with severe hunger. What is permissible for us of carrion? He said: 'If you do not take a morning draught or an evening draught from it, or incline toward it, then it is up to you.'"

There are three opinions regarding the time of the revelation of this sura.

The first: it was revealed on the day of 'Arafah. Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated from Asma bint Yazid, who said: "The whole of Surat al-Ma'idah was revealed while I was holding the rein of the she-camel of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), al-'Adba', while he was standing at 'Arafah, and she almost broke the shoulder of the camel because of its weight."

The second: it was revealed during his (ﷺ) journey in the Farewell Pilgrimage while he was riding, and his mount knelt down with him because of its weight.

The third: it was revealed on Monday in Medina. This is the opinion of Ibn Abbas, though the first opinion has been reported from him as well.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you﴾. By "the good things" He means the lawful (ḥalāl). The lawful is called "good" even when it is not pleasurable, by way of comparison with what is pleasurable. (p-15) ﴿And what you have taught of the hunting animals, training them as hunters, [is lawful for you]﴾. He means the game caught by what you have taught of the hunting animals, which are the predators among the beasts and birds of prey. They are called jawāriḥ (hunting animals, from jaraḥa, "to earn") because their owners earn by them, from the saying: "So-and-so is the jāriḥah of his family," meaning their earner. From this is the verse of al-A'shā of Banī Tha'laba:

"Many a tyrant, whose brand is marked with a hot iron, [his hunting animal] recalls the jāriḥ, what it has earned (ijtaraḥa)."

That is, what it has acquired.

As for His saying, ﴿mukallibīn﴾ (training them as hunters), there are three opinions.

The first: it means from among dogs only, and that only game caught by dogs is lawful. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī.

The second: that takklīb is one of the attributes of hunting animals, whether dogs or others, and its meaning is "incited to hunt, as dogs are incited." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbās, 'Alī ibn al-Ḥusayn, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid.

The third: that the meaning of takklīb as an attribute of the hunting animal is "teaching."

﴿You teach them from what God has taught you﴾, that is, you train them to pursue game for you, from what God has taught you of the discipline by which He has disciplined you and the characteristics of training whose ruling He has made clear to you.

As for the characteristic of training, it is that the animal is released when released, comes back when called, and holds the prey when it seizes it.

Is its refraining from eating the prey a condition for the validity of the training or not? There are three opinions. The first: it is a condition for all hunting animals, so if it eats, the game is not to be eaten. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbās and 'Aṭā'.

The second: it is not a condition for all hunting animals, and the game is eaten even if the animal has eaten from it. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Sa'd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Abū Hurayra, and Salmān.

(p-16) The third: it is a condition for the hunting animals among beasts, so the game is not eaten if they have eaten from it, but it is not a condition for hunting birds, so the game is eaten even if they have eaten from it. This is the view of al-Sha'bī, al-Nakha'ī, and al-Suddī.

There are two opinions concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse.

The first: what al-Qa'qā' ibn Ḥakīm narrated from Sulaymān ibn Abī Rāfi', from Abū Rāfi', who said: "Jibrīl came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to ask permission to enter upon him. He said, 'Come in.' He said, 'Yes, but we do not enter a house in which there is a dog.' Abū Rāfi' said: So he commanded me to kill every dog in Medina, and I killed them until I came to a woman who had a dog that was barking at her, so I left it out of mercy for her. Then I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him, and he commanded me to kill it, so I returned to the dog and killed it. Then they came and said, 'O Messenger of God, what is lawful for us of this community which you have commanded to be killed?' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) fell silent, and God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you, and what you have taught of the hunting animals, training them as hunters﴾, the verse."

The second: what has been related: "When Zayd al-Khayl came as a delegation to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said of him what he said of good, and named him Zayd al-Khayr. He said, 'O Messenger of God, among us are two men, one of whom is called Duraykh and the other is known as Abū Dujāna. They have five dogs that hunt gazelles. What do you say about their game?'" Hishām related from Ibn 'Abbās that the names of these five dogs belonging to Duraykh and Abū Dujāna were: al-Mukhtalis, Ghilāb, al-Ghunaym, Sahlab, and al-Mutaʿāṭī. He said: So God, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾, the verse.

(p-17) Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾, meaning their slaughtered animals.

﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾, meaning our slaughtered animals.

﴿And the chaste women from among the believers and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾, meaning marriage to chaste women. Regarding them there are two opinions. The first: they are the free women of both groups, whether they are chaste or immoral. Accordingly, it is not permissible to marry their female slaves. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Sha'bi, and al-Shafi'i said likewise.

The second: they are the chaste ones, whether free or slave women. Accordingly, it is permissible to marry their female slaves. This is the view of Mujahid and also al-Sha'bi, and Abu Hanifa said likewise.

Regarding the chaste women from among those who were given the Book, there are two opinions. The first: they are the covenanted women (mu'ahadat) rather than the women of the warring side (harbiyyat). This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: the people of the Book in general, from both the covenanted and the warring side. This is the view of the jurists and the majority of the early generations (al-salaf).

﴿When you have given them their wages﴾, meaning their dowries.

﴿Being chaste, not committing fornication﴾, meaning chaste, not adulterers.

﴿Nor taking secret lovers﴾: this refers to a woman who has a single lover with whom she stays in fornication.

(p-18) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾. He means: when you intend to rise to prayer, then wash your faces. In this there are three opinions.

The first: "When you rise to prayer while in a state of ritual impurity (muhdith), then wash," so the impurity is implied.

Regarding the obligation of wudu' (ablution) as a condition of prayer, this is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and the jurists (fuqaha').

The second: it is obligatory upon everyone who intends to rise to prayer to perform wudu', and it is not permissible to combine two obligatory prayers with one wudu'. This is related from 'Ali and 'Umar.

The third: it was obligatory upon everyone who rose to prayer, then it was abrogated (naskh) except for the one who is in a state of impurity. Sulayman ibn Buraydah related from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to perform wudu' for every prayer. When it was the year of the conquest, he prayed all the prayers with one wudu', and he wiped over his khuffs (leather socks). 'Umar said: 'You did something you used not to do.' He said: '(I did it deliberately, O 'Umar).'" 'Abd Allah ibn Hanzalah ibn 'Amir al-Ghasil related: "The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded wudu' at every prayer, and it was difficult for him, so he commanded the siwak (tooth-stick), and wudu' was lifted from him."

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah﴾, meaning, in truth, with regard to what His obedience requires.

﴿Witnesses in justice﴾, that is, with fairness.

Regarding this testimony there are three opinions.

The first is that it is testimony concerning the rights of people. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second is that it is testimony concerning what is done of the disobediences of servants. This is the view of some of the Basrans.

The third is testimony to the command of Allah, the Exalted, that it is true.

This verse was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ, and the exegetes differed about its occasion of revelation concerning him, on two views. One of them: "The Prophet went out to the Jews of Banu al-Nadir, seeking their help regarding a blood-money, and they resolved to kill him, so this was revealed concerning that." This is the view of Qatada and Mujahid.

Then Allah, the Exalted, reminded them of His blessings upon them in rescuing their Prophet, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Remember the blessing of Allah upon you when a people resolved to extend their hands against you, but He restrained their hands from you﴾. The second view: "Quraysh sent a man to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so Allah informed His Prophet of that, and these two verses were revealed concerning it." This is the view of al-Hasan.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, meaning, with sincerity in worship to Allah and adherence to His obedience.

﴿And We raised up from them twelve chieftains﴾. He took from each tribe of them a chieftain (naqib). Regarding the naqib there are three opinions: (p-20) The first: that he is the guarantor (daman), and this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: the trustworthy (amin), and this is the view of al-Rabi'.

The third: the witness over his people, and this is the view of Qatada.

Its root in the language: the naqib is the wide one; the chieftain of a people is the one who searches out (yunaqqibu) their conditions.

Concerning what these chieftains were sent for, there are two views. One of them: they were sent to the tyrants (al-jabbarin) to survey their conditions, and they returned with that to Musa, and they turned back from fighting them, because of what they saw of their severe might and great stature, except two of them. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: they were sent to their own people with what their covenant had been taken upon them for. This is the view of al-Hasan.

In the phrase of His, the Exalted: ﴿And you supported them﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: it means you helped them. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: you honored them. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda.

Its root meaning is prevention. Al-Farra' said: "I rebuked him (ʿazzartuhu ʿuzran) when I turned him back from wrongdoing," and from this comes ta'zir (discretionary punishment), because it prevents a return to ugliness.

His words, the Exalted: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them﴾. Its estimated reading is: "For their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them," and "mā" (ما) is an extra, superfluous particle (ṣila zā'ida).

﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾, from qaswa (hardness), which is solidity.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read qasiyya (قسية). Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: it is more intensive than qasiya. The second: it has the same meaning as qasiya.

﴿They distort words from their places﴾, meaning by alteration, substitution, and bad interpretation.

﴿And they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of﴾, meaning their share of the covenant that was taken from them.

﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: it means treachery from them. The second: it means a treacherous faction.

﴿Except a few of them, so pardon them and overlook﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: its ruling is established in forgiving and overlooking when one sees it fit. The second: it is abrogated (mansūkh). Concerning what abrogated it there are two views. The first: the words of His, the Exalted: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day﴾ [at-Tawba: 29]. This is the view of Qatada. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 5, verse 15–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾. He means: the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the stoning of adulterers.

﴿And pardons much﴾ of what is other than that.

﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾. Regarding the "light" there are two interpretations. One of them: it is Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The second: it is the Qur'an, and this is the view of some of the later scholars.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the paths of peace﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. One of them: "the paths of peace" means the way of Allah, because Allah is al-Salam (the Source of Peace), and its meaning is the religion of Allah; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: the way of safety from fear, and this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿And brings them out of darkness into light by His permission﴾. He means: from disbelief to faith, by His kindness.

﴿And guides them to a straight path﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. One of them: the path of truth, which is the religion of Allah; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: the path of Paradise in the Hereafter, and this is the view of some of the theologians (al-mutakallimin).

"Allah's Words: ﴿The Jews and the Christians said: We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones.﴾" There are three opinions regarding their statement.

The first: it is the saying of a group of Jews whom the Prophet (ﷺ) warned of the punishment of Allah and frightened with it. They said: "Do not frighten us: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones.﴾" This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the Jews claim that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Israel (Ya'qub) that "your son is the firstborn among sons," so they said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones.﴾ This is the view of al-Suddi.

Al-Hasan said: they said that in the sense of the closeness of a child to his father. This is the third opinion.

As for the Christians, there are two opinions regarding their saying this. The first: it is due to their interpretation of what is in the Gospel (Injil) of His saying: "Go to my Father and your Father." So, for that reason, they said: ﴿We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones.﴾ The second: it is due to their saying about the Messiah: "the son of Allah," and they return to this, so they made themselves the sons of Allah and His beloved ones. Allah refuted their claim with His saying: ﴿So why does He punish you for your sins?﴾ Because a father, out of his compassion, does not punish his son, nor does a lover punish his beloved.(p-٢٤)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He appointed among you prophets"﴾. There are two opinions regarding them.

The first: they are the prophets who came after Moses.

The second: they are the seventy whom Moses chose.

﴿And made you kings﴾. There are five opinions regarding this:

The first: it is because they freed themselves, when He delivered them from the enslavement imposed on them by the Qibt (the Copts). This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: it is because each one of them owned himself, his family, and his property. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: it is because they were the first of the children of Adam to own servants. This is the view of Qatadah.

As for His saying, ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾, and His saying, ﴿for it is forbidden to them﴾, this is because it was a gift from Allah, Exalted is He, to them, and then He forbade it to them after their disobedience.

﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: do not turn back from obedience to Allah to disobedience to Him.

The second: do not turn back from the land you were commanded to enter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed in it are a people of tyrants (jabbarin)"﴾. The jabbar is the one who compels people to what he wishes to force them into. From it comes jabr al-'azm (setting a broken bone), since it is like compulsion toward rectitude. It is also said that the sticks which hold the splinted limb are called jubbarah, when the hand stands straight lengthwise, because they resist just as a jabbar resists people.

It is said that the tyranny of these people reached the point that one of them took the twelve chieftains whom Moses had sent to report to him about their war, carried them together with a fruit he had brought from his orchard, came and spread them out before the king, and said: "These want to fight us." The king said: "Return to your companion and inform him of our news."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Said two men from among those who feared﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: they feared Allah. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: they feared the tyrants, yet their fear did not prevent them from speaking the truth.

﴿On whom Allah had bestowed favor﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: by granting them success in obedience.

The second: by Islam. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Regarding these two men there are two opinions:

The first: they were among the chieftains, Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yufuna. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: they were two men who were in the city of the tyrants, on whom Allah bestowed favor with Islam. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Enter upon them through the gate, and when you have entered it, you will surely be victorious﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: they only said this because they knew that Allah had prescribed it for them.

The second: they knew that Allah would give them victory over their enemies, and their fear did not prevent them from speaking the truth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let none of you be prevented by fear of people from speaking the truth when he sees it or knows it, for it does not bring one nearer to provision, nor does it delay one's term."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 5, verses 27–31:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions. The first: they are from the Children of Israel, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: they are the two sons of Adam from his own loins, namely Habil and Qabil (Cain and Abel), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid and Qatadah.

﴿When they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but was not accepted from the other﴾. The qurban (sacrifice/offering) is the act of piety intended to draw near to God's mercy, and it is on the pattern fu'lan from qurb (nearness).

Scholars differed regarding the cause for which they offered the sacrifice, on two views. The first: they did it without any cause.

The second, which is the more well-known of the two views: that it was for a cause, namely that Hawwa' (Eve) used to bear, every year, a boy and a girl, and the boy would marry the girl from the other womb. Each of the two sons of Adam, Habil and Qabil, had a twin sister. Habil wished to marry Qabil's twin, but he (Qabil) prevented him and said: "I have more right to her than you."

Scholars differed regarding the reason for his prohibition, on two views. The first: Qabil said to Habil: "I have more right to my twin than you, because we are from the birth of Paradise and you are from the birth of the earth."

The second: he prevented him from her because his twin was more beautiful than Habil's and than her own twin. So they offered a sacrifice. Qabil was a farmer and Habil was a herdsman. Habil offered a fat young lamb from the best of his property, and Qabil offered a bundle of ears of grain from the worst of his property. A white fire descended and consumed the sacrifice of Habil and left the sacrifice of Qabil. That was the sign of acceptance. There was no poor person among them upon whom one would draw near through charity; their offerings were only of this kind.

Abu Ja'far al-Tabari said: Habil's accepted lamb continued grazing in Paradise until God ransomed with it Isaac, son of Ibrahim, the one to be sacrificed.

Scholars differed regarding the cause of the acceptance of Habil's offering, on two aspects. The first: because he was more mindful of God (atqa) than Qabil, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous﴾. Here taqwa (piety) means prayer, as the commentators have mentioned.

The second: because Habil drew near with the best of his property, so it was accepted from him, while Qabil drew near with the worst of his property, so it was not accepted from him. This is the view of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and most of the commentators.

Scholars differed as to whether their offering was by the command of Adam or on their own initiative, on two views. The first: they offered by the command of Adam when they brought their dispute to him.

The second: they offered on their own initiative.

Adam had set out towards Makkah, to see it and to visit the House there, by a command he had received. He had offered the trust (amanah) of guarding his family to the heavens, and they refused it; he offered it to the earth, and it refused; he offered it to the mountains, and they refused; he offered it to Qabil, and he accepted it. Then Adam set out and returned, and found that Qabil had killed Habil, and the earth had drunk his blood. Adam wept and cursed the earth for drinking his blood, so it brought forth thorns, and it has not drunk blood since.

Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim narrated from Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani, from 'Ali, who said: When Qabil son of Adam killed his brother Habil, Adam, peace be upon him, wept over him and said:

Lines of poetry:
The lands have changed, and whoever dwells upon them,
so the face of the earth is dust-covered and ugly.
Every colored thing has changed,
and the brightness of the comely face has diminished.

He said: then Adam was answered:

O father of Habil, both have been slain together,
and the living has become like the slaughtered dead.
He came with the worst that had ever been from him,
in fear, so he came with a cry.

Scholars differed regarding Qabil, whether at the time of killing his brother he was a disbeliever or a wrongdoer (fasiq)? Some people said he was a disbeliever, while others said he was rather an evil man and a wrongdoer.

Ibn Jurayj said: The children of Adam continued to marry their sisters until four generations of fathers had passed, then he married his paternal uncle's daughter, and the marriage to sisters ended.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you stretch your hand towards me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand towards you to kill you﴾. Its meaning: if you initiate killing me, I shall not initiate with its like against you. Concerning his refraining from repelling him, there are two views. The first: restraint prevented him from it, while he was able to do so and it was permissible for him; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.

The second: it was not permissible for him to resist whoever intended (to kill him) at that time; this is the view of Mujahid and al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾. Its meaning: you will return with them. Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: that you bear the sin of my killing and your sin which is upon you from your disobediences and misdeeds; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: meaning that you bear my sin for my wrongs, and your sin for your killing of me, so you bear both of them together; this is the view of Mujahid.

Al-A'mash narrated, from 'Abdullah ibn Murrah, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of it falls upon the first son of Adam, for he was the first to establish killing."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So his soul made it easy for him to kill his brother, and he killed him﴾. The meaning of tawwa'at is fa''alat from obedience (ta'ah). Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: it means it encouraged him; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it means it adorned it for him; this is the view of Qatadah.

The third: it means it assisted him.

Habil was the first to be killed on the earth. It is said that Qabil did not know how to kill him until Iblis appeared to him and taught him. It is also said that he killed him by stealth, by dropping a rock upon him while he slept and crushing him with it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then God sent a crow digging in the earth to show him how to conceal the shame of his brother﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: it means the nakedness (awrah) of his brother. The second: the corpse of his brother, because he left it until it rotted, so the corpse was called sawah (shame).

Concerning the crow that was sent, there are two views: (p-31) The first: it was an angel in the form of a crow, which dug the earth over the shame of his brother until he learned how to bury him. The second: it was a crow that dug the earth over another crow.

﴿He said: "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the shame of my brother?" So he became one of the regretful﴾. It is said that he regretted on a basis other than that which makes repentance valid, so his repentance was not accepted from him; had he regretted on the correct basis, his repentance would have been accepted.

Ma'mar narrated, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed the two sons of Adam set an example for this nation, so take the good from them and leave their evil."

Its meaning: if you initiate killing me, I shall not initiate with its like against you. Concerning his refraining from repelling him, there are two views. The first: restraint prevented him from it, while he was able to do so and it was permissible for him; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar.

The second: it was not permissible for him to resist whoever intended (to kill him) at that time; this is the view of Mujahid and al-Hasan.

The first: that you bear the sin of my killing and your sin which is upon you from your disobediences and misdeeds; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: meaning that you bear my sin for my wrongs, and your sin for your killing of me, so you bear both of them together; this is the view of Mujahid.

Al-A'mash narrated, from 'Abdullah ibn Murrah, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of it falls upon the first son of Adam, for he was the first to establish killing."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So his soul made it easy for him to kill his brother, and he killed him﴾. The meaning of tawwa'at is fa''alat from obedience (ta'ah). Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: it means it encouraged him; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it means it adorned it for him; this is the view of Qatadah.

The third: it means it assisted him.

It is said that he regretted on a basis other than that which makes repentance valid, so his repentance was not accepted from him; had he regretted on the correct basis, his repentance would have been accepted.

Ma'mar narrated, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed the two sons of Adam set an example for this nation, so take the good from them and leave their evil."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 5, verses 27–31:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam in truth﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions. The first: they are from the Children of Israel, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: they are the two sons of Adam from his own loins, namely Habil and Qabil (Cain and Abel), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid and Qatadah.

﴿When they both offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them but was not accepted from the other﴾. The qurban (sacrifice/offering) is the act of piety intended to draw near to God's mercy, and it is on the pattern fu'lan from qurb (nearness).

Scholars differed regarding the cause for which they offered the sacrifice, on two views. The first: they did it without any cause.

The second, which is the more well-known of the two views: that it was for a cause, namely that Hawwa' (Eve) used to bear, every year, a boy and a girl, and the boy would marry the girl from the other womb. Each of the two sons of Adam, Habil and Qabil, had a twin sister. Habil wished to marry Qabil's twin, but he (Qabil) prevented him and said: "I have more right to her than you."

Scholars differed regarding the reason for his prohibition, on two views. The first: Qabil said to Habil: "I have more right to my twin than you, because we are from the birth of Paradise and you are from the birth of the earth."

The second: he prevented him from her because his twin was more beautiful than Habil's and than her own twin. So they offered a sacrifice. Qabil was a farmer and Habil was a herdsman. Habil offered a fat young lamb from the best of his property, and Qabil offered a bundle of ears of grain from the worst of his property. A white fire descended and consumed the sacrifice of Habil and left the sacrifice of Qabil. That was the sign of acceptance. There was no poor person among them upon whom one would draw near through charity; their offerings were only of this kind.

Abu Ja'far al-Tabari said: Habil's accepted lamb continued grazing in Paradise until God ransomed with it Isaac, son of Ibrahim, the one to be sacrificed.

Scholars differed regarding the cause of the acceptance of Habil's offering, on two aspects. The first: because he was more mindful of God (atqa) than Qabil, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, God accepts only from the righteous﴾. Here taqwa (piety) means prayer, as the commentators have mentioned.

The second: because Habil drew near with the best of his property, so it was accepted from him, while Qabil drew near with the worst of his property, so it was not accepted from him. This is the view of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and most of the commentators.

Scholars differed as to whether their offering was by the command of Adam or on their own initiative, on two views. The first: they offered by the command of Adam when they brought their dispute to him.

The second: they offered on their own initiative.

Adam had set out towards Makkah, to see it and to visit the House there, by a command he had received. He had offered the trust (amanah) of guarding his family to the heavens, and they refused it; he offered it to the earth, and it refused; he offered it to the mountains, and they refused; he offered it to Qabil, and he accepted it. Then Adam set out and returned, and found that Qabil had killed Habil, and the earth had drunk his blood. Adam wept and cursed the earth for drinking his blood, so it brought forth thorns, and it has not drunk blood since.

Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim narrated from Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani, from 'Ali, who said: When Qabil son of Adam killed his brother Habil, Adam, peace be upon him, wept over him and said:

Lines of poetry:
The lands have changed, and whoever dwells upon them,
so the face of the earth is dust-covered and ugly.
Every colored thing has changed,
and the brightness of the comely face has diminished.

He said: then Adam was answered:

O father of Habil, both have been slain together,
and the living has become like the slaughtered dead.
He came with the worst that had ever been from him,
in fear, so he came with a cry.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 5, verse 32–34:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Because of that﴾ means: because the son of Adam killed his brother unjustly.

﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless it be for a soul or for corruption in the land…﴾ means: whoever kills a soul unjustly, without a soul having been killed (in retaliation), so he is killed in qisas (retaliation), or for corruption in the land that makes him deserve death. Corruption in the land occurs through warfare against Allah and His Messenger, and terrorizing the highway.

(p-32) ﴿…it is as if he had killed all mankind; and whoever saves it, it is as if he had saved all mankind﴾. Regarding this there are six interpretations:

The first: it means whoever kills a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he killed all mankind; and whoever supports the hand of a prophet or a just imam, it is as if he saved all mankind. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: its meaning is that it is as if he had killed all mankind in the eyes of the one killed, and whoever saves it, rescuing it from destruction, it is as if he had saved all mankind in the eyes of the one rescued. This is the saying of Ibn Masʿud.

The third: its meaning is that the killer of a sacred soul incurs the retribution and qisas that he would incur were he to have killed all mankind, and whoever saves it by pardoning the killer, Allah gives him a reward like that of having saved all mankind. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd and his father.

The fourth: its meaning is that the killer of a sacred soul will burn in the Fire as he would burn had he killed all mankind, and whoever saves it, meaning keeps it safe from being killed, [it is as if] he has been safe from the killing of all mankind. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The fifth: that upon all people is the crime of killing as if he had killed them all, and whoever saves it by rescuing it from drowning, burning or destruction, they owe him gratitude as if he had saved them all.

The sixth: that Allah, Exalted is He, magnified its reward and its burden, so its saving [happens] by your property or your pardon. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth to cause corruption﴾. Scholars differed about whom this verse was revealed concerning, in three sayings. The first: it was revealed concerning a people of the People of the Book who had a covenant and pact with the Prophet ﷺ, but they broke the covenant and spread corruption in the land, so Allah informed His Prophet of the ruling concerning them. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning the ʿUrayniyyin, who apostatized from Islam, killed the Prophet's ﷺ shepherd, and drove off his camels. This is the saying of Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

The third: it was revealed as a report from Allah, Exalted is He, of the ruling concerning whoever wages war against Allah and His Messenger and strives upon the earth to cause corruption.

(p-33) They differed about who deserves the name "one who wages war against Allah and His Messenger", to whom the ruling of this verse applies, in three sayings. The first: it is fornication, murder and theft. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: it is one who openly commits highway robbery and brazenly engages in brigandage in the city and elsewhere. This is the saying of al-Shafiʿi, Malik and al-Awza'i.

The third: it is one who openly commits highway robbery, but not one who is brazen in the city. This is the saying of Abu Hanifa and ʿAta' al-Khurasani.

﴿…that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land﴾. Allah made this the ruling for the one who wages war, and regarding it there are two sayings. One of them: it is optional, and the imam has the choice among them, between killing, crucifying, amputating or banishing. This is the saying of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, ʿAta' and Ibrahim.

The second: it is graduated, varying according to the variation of the acts: they are killed if they killed; or crucified if they killed and took property; or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides if they took property and did not kill. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Ibn Lahiʿa narrated from Yazid ibn Abi Habib that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik asking him about this verse, and Anas wrote back informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those ʿUrayniyyin, who were of Bajila. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Jibril about retaliation regarding whoever wages war, and he said: whoever steals and terrorizes the highway, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorizing; whoever kills, kill him; and whoever kills, terrorizes the highway and makes lawful the forbidden (sexual) relations, crucify him.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾, the interpreters differed about it in four aspects: (p-34) The first: it is their banishment and removal from the lands of Islam to the lands of polytheism. This is the saying of Anas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi'.

The second: it is their removal from one city to another. This is the saying of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: it is imprisonment. This is the saying of Abu Hanifa and his companions.

The fourth: it is that they be sought so that the prescribed penalties may be enforced upon them, and they are banished. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shafiʿi and al-Layth ibn Saʿd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. Regarding this there are six sayings. The first: except those who repent from their polytheism and their striving upon the earth to cause corruption, by embracing Islam; as for Muslims, repentance does not remove a prescribed penalty that was due upon them. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: except those Muslim combatants who repent, with a guarantee of safety from the imam, before they are overpowered; as for one who repents without a guarantee, no. This is the saying of ʿAli, peace be upon him, and al-Sha'bi. al-Sha'bi narrated that Kharijah ibn Zayd went out as a combatant, terrorized the highway, shed blood and seized property, then came back repentant before he was overpowered, and ʿAli accepted his repentance and granted him a published guarantee of safety regarding the blood and property he had taken.

The third: except those who repent after they have joined the abode of war, even if he was a Muslim, then came back repentant before he was overpowered. This is the saying of ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr.

The fourth: if he was in the abode of Islam with protection, and had a faction to which he resorts, and he repented before he was overpowered, his repentance is accepted; but if he had no faction by which he could defend himself, and repented, his repentance does not remove any of his punishment. This is the saying of Ibn ʿUmar, Rabi'a and al-Hakam ibn ʿUyayna.

The fifth: that his repentance before he is overpowered removes from him the hudud of Allah, Exalted is He, but not the rights of human beings. This is the saying of al-Shafi'i.

The sixth: that his repentance before he is overpowered removes from him all rights and hudud except blood-rights. This is the doctrine of Malik.(p-35)

Allah made this the ruling for the one who wages war, and regarding it there are two sayings. One of them: it is optional, and the imam has the choice among them, between killing, crucifying, amputating or banishing. This is the saying of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, ʿAta' and Ibrahim.

The second: it is graduated, varying according to the variation of the acts: they are killed if they killed; or crucified if they killed and took property; or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides if they took property and did not kill. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Ibn Lahiʿa narrated from Yazid ibn Abi Habib that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan wrote to Anas ibn Malik asking him about this verse, and Anas wrote back informing him that this verse was revealed concerning those ʿUrayniyyin, who were of Bajila. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked Jibril about retaliation regarding whoever wages war, and he said: whoever steals and terrorizes the highway, cut off his hand for his theft and his foot for his terrorizing; whoever kills, kill him; and whoever kills, terrorizes the highway and makes lawful the forbidden (sexual) relations, crucify him.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or be banished from the land﴾, the interpreters differed about it in four aspects: (p-34) The first: it is their banishment and removal from the lands of Islam to the lands of polytheism. This is the saying of Anas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi'.

The second: it is their removal from one city to another. This is the saying of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: it is imprisonment. This is the saying of Abu Hanifa and his companions.

The fourth: it is that they be sought so that the prescribed penalties may be enforced upon them, and they are banished. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Shafiʿi and al-Layth ibn Saʿd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. Regarding this there are six sayings. The first: except those who repent from their polytheism and their striving upon the earth to cause corruption, by embracing Islam; as for Muslims, repentance does not remove a prescribed penalty that was due upon them. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: except those Muslim combatants who repent, with a guarantee of safety from the imam, before they are overpowered; as for one who repents without a guarantee, no. This is the saying of Ibn ʿUmar, Rabi'a and al-Hakam ibn ʿUyayna.

The fifth: that his repentance before he is overpowered removes from him the hudud of Allah, Exalted is He, but not the rights of human beings. This is the saying of al-Shafi'i.

The sixth: that his repentance before he is overpowered removes from him all rights and hudud except blood-rights. This is the doctrine of Malik.(p-35)

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 35–40:

Allah's words: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. In the recitation of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "As for the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands."

Allah began with the male thief before the female thief in the case of theft, and with the adulteress before the adulterer in the case of fornication, because the love of wealth is more dominant in men, and the desire for sexual enjoyment is more dominant in women. Then He made the prescribed punishment (hadd) for theft the cutting of the hand, since the hand is what is used to take property. He did not make the punishment for fornication the cutting of the male organ, even though the forbidden act is committed with it, for three reasons:

The first: the thief has a substitute for the hand that was cut off, so if he is deterred by it, he can make do with the second hand. The adulterer has no substitute for his male organ if it is cut off, so he would not have anything to replace it, even if he were deterred by its cutting.

The second: the hadd is a deterrent both for the one who receives it and for others. Cutting the hand in theft is visible, whereas cutting the male organ in fornication is hidden.

The third: cutting the male organ abolishes offspring, whereas cutting the hand does not abolish offspring.

Thieves were cut in the pre-Islamic period (Jahiliyyah). The first to rule for cutting a thief in the Jahiliyyah was al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Then Allah commanded that the thief be cut in Islam. The first thief whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cut in Islam was al-Khiyar ibn 'Adi ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf. Among the women, it was Murrah bint Sufyan ibn 'Abd al-Asad from the Banu Makhzum. He (ﷺ) said: "Even if it were Fatimah, I would cut her hand." 'Umar cut the hand of Ibn Samurah, the brother of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah.

Cutting the hand for theft is a right of Allah, the Exalted. It is not permissible to pardon it once the ruler (imam) has come to know of it, because of the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the thief of Safwan's cloak, when he ordered that his hand be cut. Safwan said: "I have pardoned him." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why did you not do so before you brought him to me? May Allah not pardon me if I pardon him."

It is related that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan was brought a group of thieves, and he cut them off until only one of them remained. He was brought forward to have his hand cut, and he said:

﻿My right hand, O Commander of the Faithful, I seek refuge for it in your pardon, lest it come to a place that disfigures it.
My hand was the beautiful one, if its trial were complete,
and the beautiful one never lacks a flaw that blemishes her.
There is no good in this world if she was the beloved,
when my left hand has parted from her, her right hand.

Mu'awiyah said: "How should I act, since I have already cut your companions?" The mother of the thief said: "O Commander of the Faithful, count it among your sins from which you repent." So he released him. This was the first prescribed punishment (hadd) left unenforced in Islam.

For the cutting to become obligatory, along with the absence of doubt (shubhah), two conditions must be met: the protected storage (hirz) and the threshold value (qadr). The jurists differed over the threshold at which the hand is cut, and the books of jurisprudence (fiqh) are more appropriate for that.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed at that point regarding the exception to cutting and its conditions, concerning one who stole from an unprotected place or stole an amount below the threshold at which the hand is cut, in Allah's words: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. Is it a general ruling ('amm) that has been specified (khass)? Or is it an unspecified ruling (mujmal) that has been explained in two ways?

One of them: it is the general ruling that has been specified.

The second: it is the unspecified ruling that has been explained.

(p-37) Then Allah said: ﴿as a recompense for what they earned﴾. The jurists differed over whether, along with cutting, the value of the stolen property must be compensated if it has been destroyed, on two views. One: there is no compensation, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. The second: compensation is obligatory, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i.

al-Kalbi mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, the thief of the coat of mail.

Allah's words: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness﴾. There are two views here regarding repentance (tawbah). One: it is like repentance from all other sins, namely regret for what has passed, and resolve not to return to it. The second: it is the hadd, and this is the view of Mujahid.

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr related that he said: "A woman stole some jewelry. The people whom she had stolen from came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this woman has stolen from us.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Cut off her right hand.' The woman said: 'Is there any repentance for me?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Today you are free from your sin as on the day your mother bore you.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness﴾."

Allah's words: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills﴾. There are two interpretations of this. One: He forgives the one who repents from his disbelief, and punishes the one who dies in his disbelief. This is the view of al-Kalbi. The second: He punishes whom He wills in this world for their sins, by killing, sinking into the earth, transformation, pains, and other kinds of His punishment, and He forgives whom He wills of them in this world through repentance, rescuing them from ruin by it and freeing them from punishment.(p-38)

He (ﷺ) said: "Even if it were Fatimah, I would cut her hand." 'Umar cut the hand of Ibn Samurah, the brother of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah.

Cutting the hand for theft is a right of Allah, the Exalted. It is not permissible to pardon it once the ruler (imam) has come to know of it, because of the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the thief of Safwan's cloak, when he ordered that his hand be cut. Safwan said: "I have pardoned him." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why did you not do so before you brought him to me? May Allah not pardon me if I pardon him."

It is related that Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan was brought a group of thieves, and he cut them off until only one of them remained. He was brought forward to have his hand cut, and he said:

﻿My right hand, O Commander of the Faithful, I seek refuge for it in your pardon, lest it come to a place that disfigures it.
My hand was the beautiful one, if its trial were complete,
and the beautiful one never lacks a flaw that blemishes her.
There is no good in this world if she was the beloved,
when my left hand has parted from her, her right hand.

Mu'awiyah said: "How should I act, since I have already cut your companions?" The mother of the thief said: "O Commander of the Faithful, count it among your sins from which you repent." So he released him. This was the first prescribed punishment (hadd) left unenforced in Islam.

For the cutting to become obligatory, along with the absence of doubt (shubhah), two conditions must be met: the protected storage (hirz) and the threshold value (qadr). The jurists differed over the threshold at which the hand is cut, and the books of jurisprudence (fiqh) are more appropriate for that.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed at that point regarding the exception to cutting and its conditions, concerning one who stole from an unprotected place or stole an amount below the threshold at which the hand is cut, in Allah's words: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. Is it a general ruling ('amm) that has been specified (khass)? Or is it an unspecified ruling (mujmal) that has been explained in two ways?

One of them: it is the general ruling that has been specified.

The second: it is the unspecified ruling that has been explained.

(p-37) Then Allah said: ﴿as a recompense for what they earned﴾. The jurists differed over whether, along with cutting, the value of the stolen property must be compensated if it has been destroyed, on two views. One: there is no compensation, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. The second: compensation is obligatory, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i.

al-Kalbi mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Tu'mah ibn Ubayriq, the thief of the coat of mail.

Allah's words: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness﴾. There are two views here regarding repentance (tawbah). One: it is like repentance from all other sins, namely regret for what has passed, and resolve not to return to it. The second: it is the hadd, and this is the view of Mujahid.

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr related that he said: "A woman stole some jewelry. The people whom she had stolen from came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this woman has stolen from us.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Cut off her right hand.' The woman said: 'Is there any repentance for me?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Today you are free from your sin as on the day your mother bore you.' Then Allah revealed: ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness﴾."

Allah's words: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills﴾. There are two interpretations of this. One: He forgives the one who repents from his disbelief, and punishes the one who dies in his disbelief. This is the view of al-Kalbi. The second: He punishes whom He wills in this world for their sins, by killing, sinking into the earth, transformation, pains, and other kinds of His punishment, and He forgives whom He wills of them in this world through repentance, rescuing them from ruin by it and freeing them from punishment.(p-38)

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah al-Ma'idah, verses 35–40:

Allah's words: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. In the recitation of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "As for the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands."

Allah began with the male thief before the female thief in the case of theft, and with the adulteress before the adulterer in the case of fornication, because the love of wealth is more dominant in men, and the desire for sexual enjoyment is more dominant in women. Then He made the prescribed punishment (hadd) for theft the cutting of the hand, since the hand is what is used to take property. He did not make the punishment for fornication the cutting of the male organ, even though the forbidden act is committed with it, for three reasons:

The first: the thief has a substitute for the hand that was cut off, so if he is deterred by it, he can make do with the second hand. The adulterer has no substitute for his male organ if it is cut off, so he would not have anything to replace it, even if he were deterred by its cutting.

The second: the hadd is a deterrent both for the one who receives it and for others. Cutting the hand in theft is visible, whereas cutting the male organ in fornication is hidden.

The third: cutting the male organ abolishes offspring, whereas cutting the hand does not abolish offspring.
