(p-82) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from heaven?"﴾ Al-Kisa'i alone read "hal tasta'ti'u rabbaka" (هَل تَّسْتَطِيع رَبَّكَ) with a *ta'* and with *idgham* (assimilation of the consonants, merging the two identical letters), and "rabbaka" in the accusative. There are two interpretations of this reading:

First: its meaning is, "Will you request obedience to your Lord in what you ask Him?" This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Second: "Are you able to ask your Lord?" This was said by Mujahid and A'isha.

The rest of the readers read "hal yasti'u rabbuka" (هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ) with a *ya'* and with *izhar* (clear articulation, without assimilation). There are three interpretations of this reading:

First: "Is your Lord able?" So this question was asked at the beginning of their affair, before their knowledge of God, Exalted is He, had become firm.

Second: its meaning is, "Will your Lord act?" This was said by al-Hasan, because they were named "disciples" (ḥawāriyyūn) only after their faith.

Third: its meaning is, "Will your Lord respond to you and obey you?"

﴿to send down upon us a table from heaven﴾ This was said by al-Suddi. Qutrub said: "A table (māʾida) is not a table unless there is food on it; if there is none, it is called a *khiwan* (a spread without food)." As for naming it *māʾida*, there are two explanations:

First: because it gives (*tamīdu*) what is upon it, that is, it bestows. Ru'ba said:

"... ... ... ∗∗∗ to the Commander of the Faithful, the one who gives (al-mumtād)"

That is, the one who seeks gifts.

Second: because of its movement (*ḥaraka*) with what is on it, from the phrase "māda al-shayʾ," meaning when a thing inclined and moved. The poet said:

"Perhaps you weep if a dove sings, while a branch of the thicket sways, inclining."

﴿He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."﴾ On this there are two views: (p-83) First: it means, "Fear the disobedience of God, if you are believers in Him." He commanded them with this because it is better than their request.

Second: it means, "Fear God in asking the prophets, either seeking to test them or seeking more signs from them, if you believe in them and affirm them, because what has established the proofs of their truthfulness suffices you from seeking more signs from them."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it."﴾ This is an excuse from them, by which they explained the reason for their request when they were forbidden from it. They said: ﴿We wish to eat from it﴾, which may have two meanings: (p-84) First: they wished to eat from it because of a need that prompted them.

Second: they wished it for blessing (*tabarruk*) and not for a need that prompted them. This is more likely, because if they had been in need, they would not have been forbidden from asking.

﴿and our hearts may be at rest﴾ This may have three meanings: First: our hearts may be at rest that God, Exalted is He, has sent you to us as a prophet.

Second: our hearts may be at rest that God, Exalted is He, has chosen us as helpers for you.

Third: our hearts may be at rest that God has answered what we asked.

﴿and that we may know that you have spoken truly to us﴾ In that you are a prophet to us, and this is according to the first meaning.

According to the second meaning: that you have spoken truly that we are helpers for you.

According to the third meaning: that God has answered what we asked.

Regarding their saying ﴿and that we may know﴾, there are two views: First: it is a knowledge newly acquired for them through this verse, after they did not have it. This is the view of those who claim that the request was made before their knowledge had become firm.

Second: they sought by this to add knowledge to their knowledge and certainty to their certainty. This is the view of those who claim that the request was made after affirmation and knowledge.

﴿and that we may be among its witnesses﴾ This may have two meanings:

First: witnesses for you before God, that you have conveyed what He sent you with to us.

Second: witnesses before those of our people who come after us, of the signs we witnessed that prove you are a prophet to them and to us.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said, "O God, our Lord, send down upon us a table from heaven."﴾ The letter *mīm* was added at the end of *Allāhumma* (O God), made heavy, as a substitute for the vocative particle, so the vocative particle cannot enter upon it; one does not say "yā Allāhumma," because the *mīm* that replaces it has taken its place. As for the poet's saying:

"What harm is there for you, whenever you say, when you glorify or declare the oneness of God, 'yā Allāhumma'? Return to us our shaykh, a Muslim, for we shall not lack of his goodness."

This is permitted because of the necessity of poetry.

Jesus asked his Lord to send down upon them the table they had asked of him. In his request there are two views: First: he granted them a favour through the request. This is the view of those who claim that the request was after the establishment of knowledge.

Second: it was a desire on his part for God, Exalted is He, to manifest his truthfulness to them. This is the view of those who claim that the request was before the establishment of knowledge.

﴿It will be a feast for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾ There are three interpretations of this:

First: we take the day on which it was sent down as a feast, which we and those after us honour. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

It has also been said that the table was sent down upon them on a Sunday, in the morning and in the evening, and for this reason they made Sunday a feast.

Second: its meaning is "a gift (*ʿāʾida*) from God upon us, and a proof for us and for those after us."

Third: meaning, "we eat from it all together, the first of us and the last of us." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿and a sign from You﴾ meaning a sign of miraculousness that indicates Your oneness. It has been said: the sign that indicates the truthfulness of Your prophets.

(p-85) Gratitude for what You have bestowed upon us of Your response. It has also been said: grant us that from Your presence.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God said, "I will indeed send it down upon you."﴾ This is a promise from God, Exalted is He, by which He answered the request of Jesus, just as Jesus's request was an answer to the disciples.

They differed concerning the sending down of the table, in three sayings:

First: it is a parable that God, Exalted is He, struck for His creatures, by which He forbids them from asking for signs from His prophets. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: they asked, and He promised them a response. Then when He said to them: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after this, I will surely punish him with a punishment I have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds﴾, they asked to be excused from it, so it was not sent down to them. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: they asked and He answered them, and they did not ask to be excused, because He did not relate their asking to be excused, and then He sent it down upon them, because He had promised them, and it is not permissible for Him to break His promise.

Those who hold this view differed concerning what was on it when it was sent down, in six sayings:

First: on it were the fruits of Paradise. This was said by Qatada.

Second: on it were bread and meat. This was said by Ammar ibn Yasir.

Third: on it were seven loaves. This was said by Ishaq ibn Abd Allah.

Fourth: on it was a fish that had the taste of every food. This was said by Ata' and Atiyya.

Fifth: on it was every food except meat. This was said by Maysara.

Sixth: two loaves and two fish; they ate from it for forty days in a single meal, and they and those with them numbered about five thousand. This was said by Juwaybir.

They were commanded to eat from it, and not to betray or to hoard. They betrayed and hoarded, so it was lifted up.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a punishment I have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds﴾, there are two views: First: it means among the worlds of their own time.

(p-86) Second: among all the worlds.

Regarding this punishment there are two views: First: that He would transform them into monkeys. This was said by Qatada.

Second: that it is a kind of punishment with which no one else will be punished, because they disbelieved after they had seen signs that no one else had seen, so they were greater in disbelief and therefore greater in punishment.

Second: that they were those appointed to preserve their laws, either by struggle (*jihād*) or by knowledge.

"We are people who fill the desert with safety, and we are the disciples when we advance in battle."

Third: its meaning is, "Will your Lord respond to you and obey you?"

First: because it gives (*tamīdu*) what is upon it, that is, it bestows. Ru'ba said:

"... ... ... ∗∗∗ to the Commander of the Faithful, the one who gives (al-mumtād)"

That is, the one who seeks gifts.

Second: because of its movement (*ḥaraka*) with what is on it, from the phrase "māda al-shayʾ," meaning when a thing inclined and moved. The poet said:

"Perhaps you weep if a dove sings, while a branch of the thicket sways, inclining."

﴿He said, "Fear God, if you are believers."﴾ On this there are two views: (p-83) First: it means, "Fear the disobedience of God, if you are believers in Him." He commanded them with this because it is better than their request.

Second: it means, "Fear God in asking the prophets, either seeking to test them or seeking more signs from them, if you believe in them and affirm them, because what has established the proofs of their truthfulness suffices you from seeking more signs from them."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They said, "We wish to eat from it."﴾ This is an excuse from them, by which they explained the reason for their request when they were forbidden from it. They said: ﴿We wish to eat from it﴾, which may have two meanings: (p-84) First: they wished to eat from it because of a need that prompted them.

Second: they wished it for blessing (*tabarruk*) and not for a need that prompted them. This is more likely, because if they had been in need, they would not have been forbidden from asking.

﴿and our hearts may be at rest﴾ This may have three meanings: First: our hearts may be at rest that God, Exalted is He, has sent you to us as a prophet.

Second: our hearts may be at rest that God, Exalted is He, has chosen us as helpers for you.

Third: our hearts may be at rest that God has answered what we asked.

﴿and that we may know that you have spoken truly to us﴾ In that you are a prophet to us, and this is according to the first meaning.

According to the second meaning: that you have spoken truly that we are helpers for you.

According to the third meaning: that God has answered what we asked.

Regarding their saying ﴿and that we may know﴾, there are two views: First: it is a knowledge newly acquired for them through this verse, after they did not have it. This is the view of those who claim that the request was made before their knowledge had become firm.

Second: they sought by this to add knowledge to their knowledge and certainty to their certainty. This is the view of those who claim that the request was made after affirmation and knowledge.

First: witnesses for you before God, that you have conveyed what He sent you with to us.

Second: witnesses before those of our people who come after us, of the signs we witnessed that prove you are a prophet to them and to us.

This is permitted because of the necessity of poetry.

Second: it was a desire on his part for God, Exalted is He, to manifest his truthfulness to them. This is the view of those who claim that the request was before the establishment of knowledge.

﴿It will be a feast for us, for the first of us and the last of us﴾ There are three interpretations of this:

First: we take the day on which it was sent down as a feast, which we and those after us honour. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

It has also been said that the table was sent down upon them on a Sunday, in the morning and in the evening, and for this reason they made Sunday a feast.

Second: its meaning is "a gift (*ʿāʾida*) from God upon us, and a proof for us and for those after us."

Third: meaning, "we eat from it all together, the first of us and the last of us." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿and a sign from You﴾ meaning a sign of miraculousness that indicates Your oneness. It has been said: the sign that indicates the truthfulness of Your prophets.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God said, "I will indeed send it down upon you."﴾ This is a promise from God, Exalted is He, by which He answered the request of Jesus, just as Jesus's request was an answer to the disciples.

They differed concerning the sending down of the table, in three sayings:

First: it is a parable that God, Exalted is He, struck for His creatures, by which He forbids them from asking for signs from His prophets. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: they asked, and He promised them a response. Those who hold this view differed concerning what was on it when it was sent down, in six sayings:

First: on it were the fruits of Paradise. This was said by Qatada.

Second: on it were bread and meat. This was said by Ammar ibn Yasir.

Third: on it were seven loaves. This was said by Ishaq ibn Abd Allah.

Fourth: on it was a fish that had the taste of every food. This was said by Ata' and Atiyya.

Fifth: on it was every food except meat. This was said by Maysara.

﴿He said: "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say"﴾, that is, to claim for myself what is not befitting of it, meaning: I am one who is nurtured and not a lord, and a worshipper and not one who is worshipped.

He began with glorification before the answer for two reasons: First: to declare Him far above what was attributed to Him.

Second: out of humility before His might and fear of His wrath.

Then he said: ﴿If I had said it, You would surely have known it﴾, so he referred that to His knowledge, the Exalted. Allah was certainly aware that he had not said it, but He said it as a rebuke to those who took Jesus as a god.

﴿You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Yours﴾. In this there are two meanings:

First: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal.

Second: You know what I know, and I do not know what You know.

As to "soul" (nafs), there are two opinions: First: that it is an expression for the whole entity.

Second: that it is an expression for a part of it, as in the saying "So-and-so killed himself."

﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen things﴾ may bear two meanings: First: the Knower of the secret and the open.

Second: the Knower of what has been and what will be.

As to the difference between ʿālim (knower) and ʿallām (all-knowing), there are two meanings: First: that the ʿallām is one whose knowledge is eternal (preceding), while the ʿālim is one whose knowledge came into being.

Second: that the ʿallām is one who knows what has been and what will be, while the ʿālim is one who knows what has been but does not know what will be.

God Almighty says: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾. Jesus did not mention this as an informing, because Allah knows it; it may bear two meanings: First: a denial of those who took a god as an object of worship.

Second: a testimony to that, against his community, regarding what He commanded them of worshipping their Lord.

The Exalted says: ﴿"Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ may bear two meanings: First: informing them that Allah is his Lord and their Lord, the same One.

Second: that it is incumbent upon him and upon them to worship one Lord, so that they do not differ regarding what they worship.

﴿And I was a witness over them while I remained among them﴾ may bear two meanings: First: meaning "a witness."

Second: a witness over them.

﴿When You caused me to die﴾: in this there are two meanings: First: that it is death.

Second: that it is His raising him up to the heaven.

﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾: in this there are two meanings: First: the Guardian over them.

Second: the Knower of them.

﴿And You are a Witness over all things﴾ may bear two meanings: First: a witness to what is present and what is absent.

Second: a witness over those who disobeyed and those who obeyed.

God Almighty says: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ may bear two meanings: First: that he said it by way of seeking their favour and compassion for them, as a servant entreats his master.

Second: that he said it by way of submission to the command of his Lord and seeking refuge from His punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 5, verse 119–120:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God said: "This is a day when the truthful shall profit from their truthfulness."﴾ He means the Day of Resurrection. The truthfulness benefited them on that day because the recompense takes place in it, although truthfulness is beneficial on all days. Regarding this truthfulness there are two opinions.

The first: their truthfulness which they had in the world benefited them in the Hereafter, and they were rewarded for it with reward. According to this view, there are two possible meanings of this truthfulness:

The first: their truthfulness in their covenants (ʿuhūd).

The second: their affirmation (taṣdīq) of God's messengers and His books.

The second opinion: it is a truthfulness that they exhibit in the Hereafter, which benefits them because they uphold the right of God in it.

According to this view, there are two possible meanings of this truthfulness:

The first: their truthfulness in bearing witness for their prophets that they conveyed the message.

The second: their truthfulness in what they testify about themselves concerning their deeds. The way it benefits them is that they avert punishment by not having concealed the testimony, so He forgives them through their acknowledgment to their prophets and against themselves.

Are they diverted from it before the station of the reckoning? There are two opinions.

And God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best what is correct.
